title: Agents & Claude Code
scopeHtml: Scope: workflow vs agent, the three wiring paths, human-in-the-loop placement, Claude Code permission modes and settings, CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks, subagents and plugins.

notes.title: Workflow or agent
notes.html:
The idea. A workflow runs steps you wrote in code. An agent gets a goal and tools and decides the path itself. Agents cost coordination overhead, extra context and more ways to fail. Climb only as needed: single call, then workflow, then agent.

Workflow Agent
steps enumerable in code goal and tools known, path unknown
per-step guardrails, standard logging non-determinism acceptable, needs transcript-level tooling

Real life. An assembly line (workflow) vs. a handyman told "fix the leak" (agent). Use the line when every unit is the same.

Tech. A cron-driven ETL pipeline vs. an on-call engineer debugging an unknown outage.

notes.title: Wiring paths
notes.html:
The idea. Three ways to run an agent, ordered by how much you hand off.

Path Who runs the loop Notes
Raw Messages API loop you full control, full maintenance
Agent SDK your process, SDK structures it your code still executes tools
Claude Managed Agents (public beta) Anthropic runs loop and sandbox agent is a versioned API resource; sessions stored server-side, so not eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA; beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01

Four steps hold on every path: register tools, scope the system prompt, handle every tool_use, and define exit conditions that do not rely on Claude volunteering to stop.

Real life. Cooking from scratch, using a meal kit, or ordering delivery. Each hands off more, and you take on different constraints (delivery cannot be hospital-sterile).

Tech. Self-hosted Kubernetes, a framework, or a fully managed PaaS.

Key facts

  • A regulated workload (PHI, ZDR) picks the path before convenience does.
  • Expect a re-expression step moving from SDK to Managed Agents, not a direct export.

notes.title: Human in the loop
notes.html:
The idea. Ask: what is the worst outcome if this step runs unchecked? Place a human gate accordingly.

Insertion point Risk
before a destructive tool call high (irreversible)
after a planning step medium (wrong plan)
on unexpected output (error, empty, out of bounds) variable

A validator that passes on one file is not a check on downstream impact. The incident pattern: the loop's exit condition ("validation passed") was scoped narrower than the harm ("a customer app depends on the old value").

Real life. A surgeon's checklist: "time-out" before the first cut, not after.

Tech. A required review on changes to the production deploy config, no matter how green CI is.

notes.title: Permission modes
notes.html:
The idea. Modes trade speed for oversight.

Mode Auto-approves Still gates Use for
default reads edits and commands new or unfamiliar work
acceptEdits reads, edits, common filesystem commands (mkdir touch rm rmdir mv cp sed) inside the working dir other shell, outside-dir and protected paths trusted local work
plan reads everything until a plan is approved research on sensitive code
auto everything, after a classifier reviews each action prod deploys, mass deletes, credential exfiltration, force-push to main (blocked by default) fewer prompts with a net (research preview)
dontAsk only pre-allowed tools and read-only auto-denies the rest locked-down CI
bypassPermissions everything, no safety checks, skips protected-path guard only catastrophic deletes disposable container or VM only

Real life. Car driving modes: learner (default), driving on your own street (acceptEdits), a satnav route preview (plan), cruise control with lane assist (auto), a locked company fleet car (dontAsk), a racetrack (bypass).

Key facts

  • The "gate" in the bypass incident was the script invocation prompt, not rm.
  • Set deny rules on sensitive directories before switching modes.

notes.title: Settings hierarchy
notes.html:
The idea. Four levels, narrowest to widest authority: user ~/.claude/settings.json, project .claude/settings.json (committed), local .claude/settings.local.json (git-ignored), and enterprise managed-settings.json (admins; cannot be overridden). Deny always beats allow, in every mode. An enterprise deny is the most durable control.

Real life. House rules, building rules, city law. You cannot opt out of city law.

Tech. Team ESLint config vs. an org-wide policy-as-code enforcement.

notes.title: CLAUDE.md, rules and hooks
notes.html:
The idea. Three ways to shape behavior, with different guarantees.

Mechanism Loads Guarantee
CLAUDE.md every session a suggestion; dilutes as it grows
Rules (.claude/rules/) paths glob in YAML frontmatter loads only when matching files are touched; no paths loads at launch like CLAUDE.md (folder placement is organizational) scoped suggestion
Hooks run your script at an event; add no context deterministic enforcement

Hook events: PreToolUse (can block with exit code 2, reason on stderr), PostToolUse (cannot block; formatters, tests, audit), UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, SessionStart, SessionEnd.

/init generates a starter CLAUDE.md; validate it. An 847-line CLAUDE.md let a one-line path restriction get ignored.

Real life. A sign saying "please don't walk on the grass" (CLAUDE.md) vs. a locked gate (hook).

Tech. A style guide in the wiki vs. a pre-commit hook that rejects the commit.

notes.title: Subagents and plugins
notes.html:
Subagents. Each runs in an isolated context and returns a summary. They start clean: no conversation history, no skills (they inherit the parent's permission context). The built-in Explore and Plan subagents skip CLAUDE.md and git status for speed; the general-purpose subagent loads both. Custom subagents live in .claude/agents and must list the skills they need.

Plugins. A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers, distributed through a marketplace (/plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>). Commands are namespaced by plugin name (/payments:run-tests), so renaming the plugin renames every command. Skills are now the recommended format (/skill-name; disable-model-invocation: true makes it explicit-only); .claude/commands/ is legacy. Admins gate sources with a managed allowlist and push one with extraKnownMarketplaces.

Real life. Hiring a contractor who has not seen your house rules (subagent), and a starter kit you hand to every new tenant (plugin).

Tech. A worker process with a fresh environment; an npm package that bundles config.

Key facts

  • Do not hard-code absolute paths or environment assumptions in a plugin.

questions.promptHtml:
A task always follows the same five steps and inputs are well constrained. What should you build?

  • A. An agent, for flexibility
  • B. A workflow, because you can enumerate the steps in code
  • C. A multi-agent orchestrator
  • D. Nothing; it cannot be automated

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Start with the simplest pattern: single call, then workflow, then agent only if the path cannot be enumerated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Agents add behavioral complexity and transcript-level observability needs. Choose an agent when you can specify the goal and tools but not the path, and inputs vary unpredictably.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare product handles PHI and needs a long-running agent. A teammate suggests Claude Managed Agents because it removes the loop and sandbox work. What is the problem?

  • A. Managed Agents cannot call tools
  • B. Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA; use the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration
  • C. Managed Agents only run for seconds
  • D. There is no problem; BAAs cover beta features

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The governing compliance constraint picks the wiring path before convenience does.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Three paths: raw Messages API loop (you own everything), Agent SDK (runs the loop in your process; you still execute tools), Managed Agents (public beta; Anthropic runs the loop and sandbox; agent defined as a versioned API resource; beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01). A BAA also excludes Console, Workbench, beta features and consumer plans.

questions.contextHtml: A config-editing agent (read_file, write_file, validate_config) was tested in a scratch directory. In a customer environment it corrected an out-of-range rate limit, validate_config passed, the loop exited. Minutes later the customer's app was throttled and failing.
questions.promptHtml:
What design step was missing?

  • A. More loop iterations
  • B. A checkpoint between "proposed change ready" and "write committed", placed by asking the worst outcome if write_file runs unchecked
  • C. A stricter schema for validate_config
  • D. Lower temperature

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blaming the validator or the loop cap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What depends on that value downstream? Is the environment reversible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore the old value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing HITL gate; validator too narrow; exit condition too narrow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Review the exit condition and the tool's blast radius.
  5. Root cause: Exit condition scoped to the file; no gate before a production write.
  6. Fix: Pause and surface proposed changes for human approval before the first live write (or a PreToolUse hook); keep a dry-run mode.
  7. Prevention: Ask the worst-case question during tool scoping, not after the first incident.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not gate every read; reserve gates for irreversible actions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Other insertion points? → After a planning step (wrong plan), and on unexpected output (error, empty, out-of-bounds).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the loop.
  • Hire: adds approval.
  • Strong hire: places gates by worst-case cost and enforces with a hook.

questions.promptHtml:
Which mode is built for locked-down CI where anything not pre-approved must be refused with no prompt queue?

  • A. acceptEdits
  • B. plan
  • C. dontAsk
  • D. bypassPermissions

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. dontAsk auto-approves only allow-listed tools plus read-only commands and auto-denies the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: default prompts on edits and commands; acceptEdits allows edits and common filesystem commands (mkdir touch rm rmdir mv cp sed) inside the working directory; plan blocks edits and commands until a plan is approved; auto lets a classifier review each action and blocks risky ones (research preview); bypassPermissions skips all prompts and the protected-path guard and is only for disposable containers or VMs.

questions.contextHtml: A developer switched to bypassPermissions to rename /v1/legacy/ endpoint references. A cleanup script matched the same pattern in /deploy/config/prod/ and deleted three files with no prompt.
questions.promptHtml:
What should have been done?

  • A. Nothing; this was unforeseeable
  • B. Set deny rules on sensitive directories first, and use auto (classifier-gated) or default/acceptEdits instead of a full bypass
  • C. Trust the agent more
  • D. Run the script in plan mode

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treating it as a model bug instead of a configuration choice.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the pattern anchored to /src/? Was an enterprise deny rule set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore from version control or backups.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-broad glob; no deny rule; bypass mode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the match in a dry run.
  5. Root cause: Over-broad pattern plus a mode with no checkpoints.
  6. Fix: B. Note the gate would have been the script invocation prompt in default mode.
  7. Prevention: Enterprise deny rule on /deploy/config/**; deny always beats allow.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not use bypass on a workstation against a live codebase.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Would acceptEdits have stopped direct rm in the working dir? → No, it auto-approves rm inside the working directory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the agent.
  • Hire: sets deny rules.
  • Strong hire: explains where the gate sat and chooses auto plus enterprise deny.

questions.promptHtml:
An administrator needs a rule denying edits to .env files that no developer or project file can override. Where does it go?

  • A. ~/.claude/settings.json
  • B. .claude/settings.json in the repo
  • C. .claude/settings.local.json
  • D. Enterprise managed-settings.json

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: D. Managed settings sit above user and project scope and cannot be overridden; deny beats allow in every mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Scope order is user, project, local project, then enterprise managed settings; managed sits on top and cannot be overridden by users or project files. A deny rule always beats an allow rule regardless of mode, so an enterprise deny is the most durable governance control. User, project and local files are all editable by developers or the repo.

questions.promptHtml:
"Run the formatter after every edit" and "never touch /legacy/tokens/" must hold every single time. How should each be enforced?

  • A. Write both in CLAUDE.md
  • B. A PostToolUse hook for the formatter and a PreToolUse hook (exit code 2) or deny rule for the protected path
  • C. A longer system prompt
  • D. A subagent

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Hooks run independently of the model's decision; CLAUDE.md is a suggestion that dilutes as it grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PreToolUse can block (exit 2, reason on stderr); PostToolUse cannot block, which suits formatters, tests and audit logging. Others: UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, SessionStart, SessionEnd. In an incident an 847-line CLAUDE.md let a one-line path restriction get ignored by dilution; keep CLAUDE.md to behavior-changing rules and path-scope the rest with .claude/rules/ using a paths glob (a rule without paths loads at launch like CLAUDE.md, regardless of folder).

questions.promptHtml:
You delegate a refactor to the built-in Explore subagent expecting it to respect your CLAUDE.md conventions. It does not. Why?

  • A. CLAUDE.md is ignored everywhere
  • B. Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status for speed; use the general-purpose subagent or a custom subagent that loads the rules
  • C. Subagents inherit skills automatically
  • D. Subagents share the parent's full history

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Subagents start clean; only the general-purpose one loads CLAUDE.md, and custom ones need skills listed explicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Subagents start from a clean slate and do not inherit conversation history or skills (they do inherit the parent's permission context). Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status to stay fast and cheap; the general-purpose subagent loads both. For work that must respect project rules, use general-purpose or a custom subagent in .claude/agents that lists the skills and rules it needs.

questions.promptHtml:
A plugin named payments ships a run-tests command. How is it invoked, and what is the portability risk?

  • A. /run-tests; no risk
  • B. /payments:run-tests; hard-coded absolute paths or environment assumptions will work for the author and fail on other machines
  • C. /plugin run-tests; plugins cannot be shared
  • D. /payments/run-tests; plugin names don't matter

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Plugin commands are namespaced by plugin name, so renaming the plugin renames every command.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers, distributed through a marketplace (/plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>). Enterprise admins gate sources with a managed allowlist and push one with extraKnownMarketplaces. Skills are now the recommended format; disable-model-invocation: true makes a skill explicit-only; .claude/commands/ is legacy.

questions.promptHtml:
User inputs vary wildly and the path to the goal cannot be listed in advance. What fits?

  • A. A fixed workflow
  • B. An agent given a goal and tools
  • C. A single prompt with no tools
  • D. A cron job

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Unenumerable paths are the case for agents; accept non-determinism and add transcript-level observability.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Climb only as needed: single call, then workflow, then agent.

questions.promptHtml:
Why must a loop have exit conditions that do not depend on Claude deciding to stop?

  • A. Claude cannot stop
  • B. Without them the agent may keep requesting tool calls beyond what the task needs
  • C. The API requires it
  • D. It improves caching

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Define when "done" means done (max iterations, success predicate).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The four loop steps are: register tools, scope the system prompt, handle every tool_use, define exit conditions.

questions.promptHtml:
What does Claude Managed Agents take off your plate?

  • A. Model selection
  • B. The iteration loop, the sandbox and tool-execution runtime, run by Anthropic server-side
  • C. Your prompts
  • D. Your evals

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. In exchange, sessions are stored server-side and it is a beta surface that can change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: It needs the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header. Skills are attached to the agent definition, not at session time.

questions.promptHtml:
A team registers 60 tools "just in case" and tool selection gets erratic. Fix?

  • A. Add 20 more descriptions
  • B. Start with the minimum tool set and add tools only when a specific capability gap is confirmed
  • C. Lower the temperature
  • D. Switch to streaming

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Selection quality degrades as the tool surface grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Too few tools is the opposite failure: the agent hallucinates a path or returns incomplete results.

questions.promptHtml:
Which is true of acceptEdits?

  • A. It auto-approves all shell commands
  • B. It auto-approves edits and common filesystem commands inside the working directory; other shell commands and protected paths still prompt
  • C. It blocks all edits
  • D. It disables deny rules

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It is scoped to paths inside the working directory.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Deny rules still win. It is not appropriate if the agent must run arbitrary scripts.

questions.promptHtml:
How does auto differ from bypassPermissions?

  • A. They are identical
  • B. auto has a separate classifier review each action and block risky ones; bypass has no checks at all
  • C. auto only reads files
  • D. bypass uses a classifier

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Want fewer prompts without losing the safety net? Use a classifier-gated mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: auto is a research preview and not a substitute for reviewing sensitive operations.

questions.promptHtml:
Project settings allow editing config/, enterprise settings deny it. What happens?

  • A. The project allow wins
  • B. The deny wins; deny beats allow in every mode and managed settings cannot be overridden
  • C. The user is prompted every time
  • D. The most recent file wins

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The most durable governance control is an enterprise deny rule.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "settings hierarchy". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
What can a PostToolUse hook NOT do?

  • A. Run a formatter
  • B. Block the tool call that just completed
  • C. Write an audit log
  • D. Trigger tests

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The call has already happened; blocking belongs in PreToolUse.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PreToolUse can exit with code 2 and write the reason to stderr as feedback the agent sees.

questions.promptHtml:
A rules file in .claude/rules/database/ has no paths frontmatter. When does it load?

  • A. Only when database files are touched
  • B. At launch, unconditionally, like CLAUDE.md; folder placement is organizational only
  • C. Never
  • D. Only in plan mode

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Scoping comes from the paths glob, not from the folder.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "claude md rules and hooks". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
Admins want a marketplace pushed to everyone and sources restricted. What do they use?

  • A. Individual user settings
  • B. A managed allowlist for sources plus extraKnownMarketplaces in managed settings to register it
  • C. A README
  • D. A hook

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The allowlist alone only restricts what users may add; it does not register a marketplace.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Managed scope sits above user and project settings, so users cannot override it.
